title: Masquerading: Overwrite Process Arguments
summary: Overwriting process arguments is a Linux-oriented hiding technique in which a running program rewrites its own command-line memory so that process listings show something benign. The kernel stores the argument strings in the process address space and exposes them through the proc filesystem, and ordinary tools read that same region, so a program that clears the strings and writes a fake first argument changes what an analyst sees without needing elevated privilege. Two artefacts usually survive: the executable path and its on-disk identity, since the binary that was executed is unchanged, and any log that captured the command line at process creation time before the rewrite happened. Detection therefore compares the visible command line with the executable it belongs to, looks for entries whose reported name does not match that binary, and relies on audit or process accounting telemetry that records arguments at execution rather than on demand. Legitimate programs do sometimes change their displayed name, so context such as the binary path, its hash, the user and the parent process should carry the decision.

beginner.definition: This is a trick where a running program changes the command line it shows to other programs. On Linux the system keeps each program's start command in memory. The program can overwrite that memory. Tools that list processes then show a harmless command instead.
beginner.whyItMatters: When you investigate a machine, the process list is often your first stop. If the command names are fake, your first stop lies to you. Investigators may skip a program that looks like a normal system task. The trick needs no special permission, so a normal user can do it. You must check more than the visible command.
howItWorks: The program starts normally, and the system stores its arguments in memory.
The program writes empty bytes over all of those stored argument strings.
This removes the evidence of how it was originally started.
It then writes a false, harmless looking command into the same memory area.
Tools that read the proc filesystem now display the false command.
The real executable file, and logs recorded at start time, do not change.
beginner.example: Picture a hotel guest book at the night desk. A guest crosses out their real name and writes room service beside it. The person is still standing there, and the room key they hold is real. Only the desk record has been altered.
takeaways: The visible command line can disagree with the program that is actually running.
Compare process names with their executable paths and hashes.
Prefer logs captured when a process starts over data read later.

objectives: Explain where Linux keeps a process command line and how it is exposed.
Describe why rewriting that memory needs no elevated privilege.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent masquerading technique.
Identify the artefacts that still reveal the original launch.
Describe how to compare displayed names with executable identities.
